extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying obviousness rationales (including 'obvious to try', cross-field adaptations, and TSM) when examining patent claims; specifies the factual findings examiners must make under Graham and case law. Focused on how to justify or reject claims for obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try applicability (KSR standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obvious-to-try may support a conclusion of obviousness when “there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions” and a person of ordinary skill “has good reason to pursue the known options” such that success is reasonably expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should find that the prior art suggested a finite, identifiable set of predictable solutions and that a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success in trying those options. Examples: Alza (sustained-release oxybutynin) — although not absolutely predictable, the prior art suggested a finite number of ways and reasonable expectation of success supported obviousness. Cite KSR: when these conditions exist, 'obvious to try' may show obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try is improper when prior art gives no indication which parameters are critical or when numerous possible choices exist
rubrics_metrics.description: One class identified by Kubin: 'when what would have been “obvious to try” would have been to vary all parameters or try each of numerous possible choices until one possibly arrived at a successful result, where the prior art gave either no indication of which parameters were critical or no direction as to which of many possible choices is likely to be successful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern for obvious-to-try. If the prior art does not narrow the options or indicate which choices are likely to work, an obvious-to-try rationale is erroneous. Examples/case law: Kubin (nucleic acid) and O’Farrell; Takeda and Ortho‑McNeil illustrate that numerous options or lack of reason to select a particular starting point defeat an obvious-to-try rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try is improper when it would require exploring a new technology or general approach with only general guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Second Kubin class: obvious-to-try is improper 'when what was “obvious to try” was to explore a new technology or general approach that seemed to be a promising field of experimentation, where the prior art gave only general guidance as to the particular form of the claimed invention or how to achieve it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art provides only broad or speculative guidance about a new field or approach (no specific, predictable solutions), do not base obviousness on 'obvious to try.' Examples: Kubin discussion; Rolls‑Royce (fan blade) — nothing in prior art suggested the specific change, so it would not have presented itself as an option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large number of options does not alone show nonobviousness; consider whether prior art narrows options
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of a large number of options in the art does not in and of itself lead to nonobviousness. Where prior art teachings lead the skilled artisan toward a narrower set of options, that reduced set is the appropriate one to consider for an obvious-to-try analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether prior art funnels the formulator/artist to particular predictable options despite the broader universe of possibilities. Example: Bayer (drospirenone micronized pill) — prior art funneled the formulator toward two options (normal pill or enteric-coated), enabling an obvious-to-try conclusion. By contrast, when the prior art dissuades selecting the closest compound (Takeda) or renders success unpredictable, nonobviousness may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success (predictability requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of reasonable expectation of success is required for obvious-to-try and many obviousness rationales; unpredictability or unexpected results can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must evaluate whether, at the time of the invention, a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation that the claimed approach would work. Lack of predictability, serendipitous discoveries, or unexpected therapeutic advantages (examples: Takeda, Ortho‑McNeil, Sanofi) support nonobviousness. Conversely, routine methods or predictable application of known techniques (examples: Morella/Sambrook sequencing and isolation leading to Kubin rejection) can support a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sense may inform obviousness if explained with sufficient reasoning and factual support
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense has long been recognized to inform the analysis of obviousness, but must be applied with a reasoned explanation and factual foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner may invoke common sense where the record provides a factual basis; avoid conclusory generalizations. Cases: Perfect Web (application of common sense with reasoning), In re Bozek (reliance on common knowledge), In re Zurko and Arendi (require a factual foundation and reasoned analysis). Identify specific record evidence or sound reasoning that shows why 'common sense' supplies the missing teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field may prompt predictable variations in another (design incentives / market forces) — five required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject based on adaptation of known work from one field to another, Office personnel must resolve Graham factual inquiries and articulate the following findings: (1) prior art included a similar or analogous device/method/product; (2) design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation; (3) differences between the claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations or principles in the prior art; (4) one of ordinary skill, in view of the incentives/forces, could have implemented the claimed variation and it would have been predictable; and (5) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rationale is that market/design pressures could have prompted predictable variation. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: Dann (data processing analogy), Leapfrog (combining older mechanical toy with modern electronics), KSR (pedal assembly adaptation). Examiners must explicitly state and support each of the five findings when relying on this rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation (TSM) to modify or combine — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on a motivation-to-combine rationale, Office personnel must resolve Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) a finding that there was some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (in the references or general knowledge) to modify or combine; (2) a finding that there was a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) whatever additional Graham-based findings are necessary to explain the conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale supports the conclusion that a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine teachings to achieve the claimed invention with a reasonable expectation of success. If any of these findings cannot be made, TSM cannot support an obviousness rejection. Case law: DyStar, In re Kahn, and discussion in Perfect Web illustrating how TSM and common sense interact under KSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve Graham factual inquiries before applying obviousness rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying any of the above rationales (obvious-to-try, cross-field adaptation, TSM, common sense), Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries (scope and content of the prior art; differences between the prior art and the claims; level of ordinary skill in the art; and objective indicia/secondary considerations) and make any additional factual findings necessary in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP repeatedly instructs examiners to place the inquiry 'in the context of the subject matter at issue' and to make explicit Graham findings. Many of the listed rationales are contingent on those factual findings; examiners must articulate them in the record with supporting evidence and reasoning (examples throughout the cited decisions: KSR, Abbott, Takeda, Perfect Web).
